question: A lumbar puncture yields: opening pressure 340 mmH₂O, turbid CSF, WBC 2,800 cells/µL (90% neutrophils), protein 280 mg/dL, glucose 18 mg/dL (blood glucose 90 mg/dL). Which diagnosis is most consistent with this CSF profile?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Viral meningitis typically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis (<500 WBC), mildly elevated protein (50–150 mg/dL), and normal glucose. This CSF is far too inflammatory for viral meningitis.

Correct. This CSF profile is classic for bacterial meningitis: high neutrophilic pleocytosis (>1,000), markedly elevated protein (>100 mg/dL), and low CSF:blood glucose ratio (<0.3 — here 18/90 = 0.20). Turbidity and raised opening pressure further confirm bacterial aetiology.

TBM shows lymphocytic pleocytosis (100–500), elevated protein (100–500 mg/dL), low glucose, and characteristically forms a cobweb clot. This acute high-neutrophil picture is more consistent with bacterial meningitis.
Cryptococcal meningitis typically shows minimal pleocytosis, high opening pressure, and India ink positivity. A neutrophilic count of 2,800 cells points to bacterial meningitis.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the CSF profiles: bacterial meningitis = neutrophilic pleocytosis + protein >100 mg/dL + glucose <45 mg/dL (CSF:serum ratio <0.4). This profile — 2,800 neutrophils, protein 280, glucose 18 — is unambiguously bacterial.

Well done. Key CSF discriminators: bacterial (neutrophils, protein >100, glucose <45 or CSF:serum <0.4); viral (lymphocytes, protein mildly raised, normal glucose); TBM (lymphocytes, low glucose, fibrin clot); cryptococcal (India ink +, minimal cells, high pressure).
